stem: Two different liquids of density \(\rho_1\) and \(\rho_2\) exert the same pressure at a certain point. What will be the ratio of the heights of the respective liquid columns?
solution:
Let \(h_1\) be the height of the liquid of density \(\rho_1\). Then the pressure exerted by the liquid of density \(\rho_1\) is \(p_1 = h_1\rho_1 g\). Similarly, let \(h_2\) be the height of the liquid of density \(\rho_2\). Then the pressure exerted by the liquid of density \(\rho_2\) is \(p_2 = h_2\rho_2 g\).
Both liquids exert the same pressure, therefore we write,
\(p_1 = p_2\)
\(\therefore h_1\rho_1 g = h_2\rho_2 g\) or, \(\dfrac{h_1}{h_2} = \dfrac{\rho_2}{\rho_1}\)
**Alternate method:**
For a given value of \(p = h\rho g = \) constant, as \(g\) is constant. So the height is inversely proportional to the density of the fluid \(\rho\). In this case, since pressure is constant, height is inversely proportional to density of the liquid.

stem: A swimmer is swimming in a swimming pool at 6 m below the surface of the water. Calculate the pressure on the swimmer due to water above. (Density of water \(= 1000\) kg/m\(^3\), \(g = 9.8\) m/s\(^2\))
solution:
Given,
\(h = 6\) m, \(\rho = 1000\) kg/m\(^3\), \(g = 9.8\) m/s\(^2\)
\(p = h\rho g = 6 \times 1000 \times 9.8 = 5.88 \times 10^{4}\) N/m\(^2\)
(Which is nearly 0.6 times the atmospheric pressure!)

stem: A hydraulic brake system of a car of mass 1000 kg having speed of 50 km/h, has a cylindrical piston of radius of 0.5 cm. The slave cylinder has a radius of 2.5 cm. If a constant force of 100 N is applied on the brake what distance the car will travel before coming to stop?
solution:
Given,
\(F_1 = 100\) N, \(A_1 = \pi(0.5 \times 10^{-2})^2\) m\(^2\), \(A_2 = \pi(2.5 \times 10^{-2})^2\) m\(^2\), \(F_2 = ?\)
By Pascal's Principle,
\(\dfrac{F_2}{A_2} = \dfrac{F_1}{A_1}\)
\(F_2 = \dfrac{100 \times \pi (2.5 \times 10^{-2})^2}{\pi (0.5 \times 10^{-2})^2} = 2500\) N
Acceleration of the car \(= a = F_2/m = 2500/1000 = 2.5\) m/s\(^2\). Using Newton's equation of motion,
\(v^2 = u^2 - 2as\) where final velocity \(v = 0\), \(u = 50\) km/h
\(s = \left(\dfrac{50 \times 1000}{3600}\right)^2 \times \dfrac{1}{(2 \times 2.5)} = 38.58\) m

stem: A beaker of radius 10 cm is filled with water. Calculate the force of surface tension on any diametrical line on its surface. Surface tension of water is 0.075 N/m.
solution:
Given,
\(L = 2 \times 10 = 20\) cm \(= 0.2\) m
\(T = 0.075\) N/m
We have,
\(T = \dfrac{F}{L}\)
\(\therefore F = TL = 0.075 \times 0.2 = 0.015 = 1.5 \times 10^{-2}\) N

stem: Calculate the work done in blowing a soap bubble to a radius of 1 cm. The surface tension of soap solution is \(2.5 \times 10^{-2}\) N/m.
solution:
Given
\(T = 2.5 \times 10^{-2}\) N/m
Initial radius of bubble \(= 0\) cm
Final radius of bubble, \(r = 1\) cm \(= 0.01\) m
Initial surface area of soap bubble \(= 0\)
(A soap bubble has two surfaces, outer surface and inner surface).
Final surface area of soap bubble is,
\(A = 2 \times (4\pi r^2) = 8\pi r^2\)
\(\therefore\) change in area \(= dA = A - 0 = 8\pi r^2 = 0.002514\) m\(^2\)
\(\therefore\) work done \(= T \times dA = 2.5 \times 10^{-2} \times 0.251 \times 10^{-2} = 6.284 \times 10^{-5}\) J

stem: What should be the diameter of a water drop so that the excess pressure inside it is 80 N/m\(^2\)? (Surface tension of water \(= 7.27 \times 10^{-2}\) N/m)
solution:
Given
\(p_{\text{i}} - p_{\text{o}} = 80\) N/m\(^2\)
\(T = 7.27 \times 10^{-2}\) N/m
We have, for a **drop** (a single liquid-air surface),
\((p_{\text{i}} - p_{\text{o}}) = \dfrac{2T}{r}\)
\(\therefore r = \dfrac{2T}{p_{\text{i}} - p_{\text{o}}} = \dfrac{2 \times 7.27 \times 10^{-2}}{80} = 1.818 \times 10^{-3}\) m
\(\therefore d = 2r = 3.636 \times 10^{-3}\) m \(= 3.636\) mm

stem: A capillary tube of radius \(5 \times 10^{-4}\) m is immersed in a beaker filled with mercury. The mercury level inside the tube is found to be \(8 \times 10^{-3}\) m below the level of reservoir. Determine the angle of contact between mercury and glass. Surface tension of mercury is 0.465 N/m and its density is \(13.6 \times 10^{3}\) kg/m\(^3\). (\(g = 9.8\) m/s\(^2\))
solution:
Given,
\(r = 5 \times 10^{-4}\) m
\(h = -8 \times 10^{-3}\) m
\(T = 0.465\) N/m
\(g = 9.8\) m/s\(^2\)
\(\rho = 13.6 \times 10^{3}\) kg/m\(^3\)
we have,
\(T = \dfrac{hr\rho g}{2\cos\theta}\)
\(\therefore 0.465 = \dfrac{-8 \times 10^{-3} \times 5 \times 10^{-4} \times 13.6 \times 10^{3} \times 9.8}{2\cos\theta}\)
\(\therefore \cos\theta = \dfrac{-40 \times 9.8 \times 13.6 \times 10^{-4}}{2 \times 0.465}\)
\(\therefore -\cos\theta = 0.5732\)
\(\therefore \cos(\pi - \theta) = 0.5732\)
\(\therefore 180^\circ - \theta = 55^\circ\,2'\)
\(\therefore \theta = 124^\circ\,58'\)

stem: A steel ball with radius 0.3 mm is falling with velocity of 2 m/s at a time \(t\), through a tube filled with glycerin, having coefficient of viscosity 0.833 N s/m\(^2\). Determine viscous force acting on the steel ball at that time.
solution:
Given
\(r = 0.3\) mm \(= 0.3 \times 10^{-3}\) m, \(v = 2\) m/s, \(\eta = 0.833\) N s/m\(^2\).
We have, \(F = 6\pi\eta r v\)
\(F = 6 \times 3.142 \times 0.833 \times 0.3 \times 10^{-3} \times 2\)
Therefore, \(F = 9.422 \times 10^{-3}\) N

stem: A spherical drop of oil falls at a constant speed of 4 cm/s in steady air. Calculate the radius of the drop. The density of the oil is 0.9 g/cm\(^3\), density of air is 0.0013 g/cm\(^3\) and the coefficient of viscosity of air is \(1.8 \times 10^{-4}\) poise, (\(g = 980\) cm/s\(^2\))
solution:
Given,
\(v = 4\) cm/s
\(\eta = 1.8 \times 10^{-4}\) Poise
\(\rho = 0.9\) g/cm\(^3\)
\(\sigma = 0.0013\) g/cm\(^3\)
We have,
\(\eta = \dfrac{2}{9}\dfrac{r^2(\rho - \sigma)g}{v}\)
\(r = \sqrt{\dfrac{9\eta v}{2(\rho - \sigma)g}}\)
\(r = \sqrt{\dfrac{9 \times 1.8 \times 10^{-4} \times 4}{2 \times (0.9 - 0.0013) \times 980}}\)
\(r = \sqrt{\dfrac{6.48 \times 10^{-3}}{1761.4}} = \sqrt{3.679 \times 10^{-6}}\)
\(\therefore r = 1.918 \times 10^{-3}\) cm
(Check: substituting \(r = 1.918 \times 10^{-3}\) cm back into \(v = \dfrac{2}{9}\dfrac{r^2(\rho - \sigma)g}{\eta}\) returns \(v = 4\) cm/s, the speed given in the question.)

subtopic: Equation of Continuity and Bernoulli's Equation
stem: As shown in the given figure, a piston of cross sectional area 2 cm\(^2\) pushes the liquid out of a tube whose area at the outlet is 40 mm\(^2\). The piston is pushed at a rate of 2 cm/s. Determine the speed at which the fluid leaves the tube.
solution:
Given,
\(A_1 = 2\) cm\(^2 = 2 \times 10^{-4}\) m\(^2\)
\(v_1 = 2\) cm/s \(= 2 \times 10^{-2}\) m/s
\(A_2 = 40\) mm\(^2 = 40 \times 10^{-6}\) m\(^2\)
From equation of continuity, \(A_1 v_1 = A_2 v_2\)
Therefore,
\(v_2 = \dfrac{A_1 v_1}{A_2} = \dfrac{2 \times 10^{-4} \times 2 \times 10^{-2}}{40 \times 10^{-6}} = 0.1\) m/s

subtopic: Equation of Continuity and Bernoulli's Equation
stem: The given figure shows a streamline flow of a non-viscous liquid having density 1000 kg/m\(^3\). The cross sectional area at point A is 2 cm\(^2\) and at point B is 1 cm\(^2\). The speed of liquid at the point A is 5 cm/s. Both points A and B are at the same horizontal level. Calculate the difference in pressure at A and B.
solution:
Given,
\(\rho = 1000\) kg/m\(^3\), \(A_1 = 2\) cm\(^2 = 2 \times 10^{-4}\) m\(^2\), \(A_2 = 1\) cm\(^2 = 10^{-4}\) m\(^2\), \(v_1 = 5\) cm/s \(= 5 \times 10^{-2}\) m/s and \(h_1 = h_2\)
From the equation of continuity,
\(A_1 v_1 = A_2 v_2\)
\(\therefore v_2 = \dfrac{A_1 v_1}{A_2} = \dfrac{2 \times 10^{-4} \times 5 \times 10^{-2}}{10^{-4}} = 0.1\) m/s \(= 10\) cm/s
By Bernoulli's equation,
\((P_1 - P_2)\,dV = \dfrac{1}{2}\rho\,dV(v_2^2 - v_1^2) + \rho\,dV g(h_2 - h_1)\)
(since \(h_2 - h_1 = 0\))
\((P_1 - P_2)\,dV = \dfrac{1}{2}\rho\,dV(v_2^2 - v_1^2)\)
\(P_1 - P_2 = \dfrac{1}{2} \times 1000 \times \left[(0.1)^2 - (0.05)^2\right]\)
\(= 500 \times 0.0075\)
\(P_1 - P_2 = 3.75\) Pa
(The speeds must be in m/s here, to match \(\rho\) in kg/m\(^3\); A is the wider section, so the pressure at A is the greater of the two.)

stem: Doors of a dam are 20 m below the surface of water in the dam. If one door is opened, what will be the speed of the water that flows out of the door? (\(g = 9.8\) m/s\(^2\)), specific gravity of mercury \(= (\rho_{Hg}/\rho_w) = 13.6\)
solution:
Given, \(h = 20\) m
From Torricelli's law,
\(v = \sqrt{2gh} = \sqrt{2 \times 9.8 \times 20} = \sqrt{392} = 19.79\) m/s

stem: Water flows through a tube as shown in the given figure. Find the difference in mercury level, if the speed of flow of water at point A is 2 m/s and at point B is 5 m/s. (\(g = 9.8\) m/s\(^2\), specific gravity of mercury \(= 13.6\))
solution:
Given, \(v_1 = 2\) m/s, \(v_2 = 5\) m/s
We have, Pressure difference in water generates level difference for the mercury in the manometer.
\(\Delta P = \dfrac{1}{2}\rho_w(v_2^2 - v_1^2) = h\rho_{Hg}g\)
\(\therefore h = \dfrac{(v_2^2 - v_1^2)}{2g\left(\dfrac{\rho_{Hg}}{\rho_w}\right)} = \dfrac{25 - 4}{2 \times 9.8 \times 13.6} = 0.07878\) m
\(= 7.878\) cm
